metadata.research_goal: Create backend-ready cycling knowledge for discipline profiles, race tactics, route and weather context, terrain decisions, drafting, paceline, attacks, lead-outs, event-week preparation, sport IQ, physical demands, load risks, and planning implications across road, criterium, time trial, track, mountain bike, gravel, cyclocross, BMX, and triathlon cycling.
metadata.scope: Discipline and tactics research only. Power-zone programming, beginner safety instruction, bike-fit diagnosis, and strength programming are included only where they directly change tactical choice, event-week planning, discipline profile, or backend load-risk rules.
metadata.source_method: Original synthesis from international and national federation resources, official competition-rule repositories, reputable coaching/racing education, and peer-reviewed sport-science sources. No long prose is copied.
metadata.rule_context_note: Competition rules, draft-legal status, equipment legality, and course formats vary by federation, event, category, and year. Backend rule logic should store event-rule context instead of hard-coding one universal rule set.

key_concepts.name: Discipline Changes The Game Model
key_concepts.summary: Cycling tactics cannot be stored as one generic road-riding model. Road races, criteriums, time trials, track events, MTB, gravel, cyclocross, BMX, and triathlon bike legs reward different blends of drafting, pacing, positioning, handling, terrain reading, and risk control.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Every tactic, workout, and race-prep recommendation should be keyed by discipline and event format before intensity or session detail is selected.

key_concepts.name: Drafting Is A Tactical Resource
key_concepts.summary: Shelter from aerodynamic drag changes energy cost, attack timing, paceline cooperation, lead-out structure, and triathlon legality. Drafting can be helpful, illegal, irrelevant, or dangerous depending on discipline and event rules.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Store draft_allowed, draft_effective, draft_skill_required, and draft_risk flags by event context.

key_concepts.name: Positioning Is Energy Management
key_concepts.summary: A rider's place in a group determines wind shelter, braking frequency, crash exposure, access to attacks, and ability to enter corners, climbs, technical sections, or feed zones safely.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Race-IQ records should treat positioning as a trainable skill, not only as a tactical instruction given on race day.

key_concepts.name: Route Context Selects Decisive Moments
key_concepts.summary: Climbs, descents, corners, crosswind roads, gravel sectors, singletrack, barriers, rhythm sections, technical turns, aid stations, and transition areas create predictable moments where races split or mistakes compound.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Plans should store route features and rehearse likely decisive segments rather than prescribe generic intervals only.

key_concepts.name: Wind Turns Roads Into Tactics
key_concepts.summary: Headwind discourages solo efforts, tailwind can reward committed attacks, and crosswind creates shelter scarcity and echelon risk. Wind direction can change whether a road segment is for recovery, attack, or survival.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Use wind direction and exposed-road flags to alter pacing, attack, and group-positioning advice.

key_concepts.name: Climbing Reduces Bunch Shelter
key_concepts.summary: On steep or slow climbs, drafting benefit drops and sustainable power, power-to-weight, cadence, traction, and pacing matter more. Climbs often expose riders who have been hiding efficiently on flat roads.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Climb tactics should shift from pack-shelter logic to power pacing, line choice, cadence, and summit positioning.

key_concepts.name: Descending Is Skill And Risk
key_concepts.summary: Descending can create or erase gaps, but mistakes have high crash cost. Braking timing, line choice, vision, surface reading, and risk tolerance determine whether descending is a tactic or a liability.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Only assign aggressive descending tactics to riders with demonstrated handling readiness and appropriate course familiarity.

key_concepts.name: Criteriums Amplify The Accordion Effect
key_concepts.summary: Repeated corners make riders at the back brake harder, accelerate harder, and experience more surges. A technically good rider near the front saves energy even at the same average speed.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Crit readiness should include cornering, surge tolerance, and front-third positioning skill, not only FTP or sprint power.

key_concepts.name: Time Trial Is Pacing Under Constraint
key_concepts.summary: Time trials remove most group tactics and replace them with aerodynamic discipline, pacing, line choice, legal overtaking, controlled starts, and terrain-adjusted effort.
key_concepts.backend_translation: TT sessions should include aero-position tolerance, power smoothing, race-position fueling, and course-specific pacing.

key_concepts.name: Track Events Are Not One Discipline
key_concepts.summary: Track sprint, keirin, team sprint, individual pursuit, team pursuit, points race, elimination, omnium, and Madison demand different tactical timing, energy systems, rotation behavior, and bike-handling confidence.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Backend track profiles should split sprint-event, pursuit-event, and bunch-endurance records before assigning training or tactics.

key_concepts.name: Off-Road Tactics Are Traction And Flow
key_concepts.summary: MTB, gravel, and cyclocross tactics depend on surface grip, tire choice, line selection, passing windows, braking control, obstacle flow, and preserving momentum.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Off-road records need surface, traction, tire, obstacle, and technical-fatigue fields, not only distance and elevation.

key_concepts.name: Cyclocross Is Repeated Transition Racing
key_concepts.summary: Cyclocross rewards repeated accelerations, corner exits, dismounts, remounts, running sections, barrier timing, mud or sand handling, pit decisions, and course-memory under fatigue.
key_concepts.backend_translation: CX training records should include transition skill density and race-pace technical repetition, not only threshold intervals.

key_concepts.name: BMX Is Start Position And Track Speed
key_concepts.summary: BMX racing is decided by gate reaction, first-straight acceleration, pump and jump rhythm, berm position, passing choices, and repeated heats rather than aerobic pack tactics.
key_concepts.backend_translation: BMX profiles should emphasize starts, sprint power, track skills, heat recovery, and crash-risk gates.

key_concepts.name: Triathlon Bike Preserves The Run
key_concepts.summary: The fastest bike split is not always the best race strategy. Triathlon cycling must respect draft legality, aero-position tolerance, nutrition, transition, heat, and the need to run effectively afterward.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Triathlon bike records should include run-preservation and total multisport load fields.

key_concepts.name: Race Week Removes Novelty
key_concepts.summary: As competition approaches, tactical rehearsal, equipment checks, course recon, fueling practice, and freshness matter more than new workouts, new bike positions, or untested race equipment.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Event-week planning should gate novelty, reduce fatigue, confirm logistics, and rehearse only the highest-value race decisions.

key_concepts.name: Field Size Changes Tactical Space
key_concepts.summary: Small fields can make moves easier to monitor and recovery harder to hide; large fields create more draft, traffic, crashes, and positioning battles. The same tactic can be sensible in one field and wasteful in another.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Race plans should store field_size_class and modify attack, positioning, and risk-control recommendations.

example_values.road_race: mass-start endurance race with drafting, terrain-based selection, attacks, breakaways, sprint or climb finishes
example_values.criterium: short-lap road race with repeated corners, accelerations, positioning, and sprint/late-attack decisions
example_values.time_trial: solo or team pacing event where aerodynamic position and legal passing replace bunch tactics
example_values.track_sprint: velodrome event centered on acceleration, timing, position, and maximal power
example_values.mtb_xco: technical off-road lap race with repeated high-intensity climbs and descents
example_values.bmx_race: start-gate sprint over jumps and berms with moto-based race format
example_values.triathlon_non_draft_bike: steady aero bike leg where pacing and fueling must preserve the run

technical_models.name: Drafting Context Model
technical_models.backend_use: Decide whether to teach drafting, paceline, echelon, solo pacing, or non-drafting separation rules.

technical_models.name: Race Phase Model
technical_models.backend_use: Attach tactical rules to phase instead of presenting every tactic at all times.

technical_models.name: Route Feature Model
technical_models.backend_use: Generate route-aware race plans, interval simulations, warm-up priorities, and skill drills.

conditions.headwind: prioritize shelter, avoid unsupported solo efforts unless selection or team goal justifies cost
conditions.tailwind: attacks and breakaways can carry speed; sprint lead-outs may need earlier commitment
conditions.crosswind: position toward shelter side, anticipate echelons and splits, avoid being trapped on exposed edge
conditions.gusty_or_wet: increase handling margin and lower risky overlapping wheels

technical_models.name: Lead-Out Model
technical_models.backend_use: Assign sprint-finish tactics based on rider role, team support, and finish geometry.

technical_models.name: Track Event Family Model
technical_models.backend_use: Split track tactics into acceleration/timing, rotation/pacing, and bunch-positioning records.

technical_models.name: Cyclocross Transition Model
technical_models.backend_use: Plan race-pace technical repetitions and tactical decisions around obstacles, mud, sand, stairs, and pits.

technical_models.name: BMX Heat Model
technical_models.backend_use: Model BMX race preparation around starts, track features, moto progression, and repeated high-power efforts.

technical_models.name: Triathlon Bike-Leg Model
technical_models.backend_use: Plan cycling work that supports whole-race triathlon performance rather than isolated bike split chasing.

tactical_rules.rule: In a road race or fast group, prioritize stable shelter and predictable movement before spending energy in the wind.
Paceline efficiency depends on smooth speed, steady pulls, clear communication, and predictable rotations more than maximal pull strength.
tactical_rules.level_gate: Do not assign tight paceline work until the rider can hold a straight line, look ahead, signal, and avoid wheel overlap.

tactical_rules.rule: A rider should not chase every move. Evaluate threat, team representation, course position, wind, rider match, and remaining distance before responding.
tactical_rules.backend_condition: If repeated high-power responses are accumulating without tactical payoff, recommend patience, teammate use, or counterattacking instead of direct chasing.

tactical_rules.rule: A breakaway is stronger when the riders are committed, complementary, represented by key teams, and able to rotate without passengers disrupting pace.
tactical_rules.backend_use: Breakaway advice should include composition and chase likelihood, not only current gap size.

tactical_rules.rule: A bridge attempt should be decisive enough to reach the move without towing the whole bunch, or delayed until terrain, wind, or counters create a better opportunity.
tactical_rules.risk_flag: Half-bridging wastes anaerobic capacity and can leave the rider exposed between groups.

tactical_rules.rule: A lead-out plan should be built from finish geometry, wind, corner count, team size, and sprinter jump duration rather than a fixed distance.
tactical_rules.backend_use: Store finish_gradient, final_corner_distance, wind, and available_leadout_riders before assigning sprint timing.

tactical_rules.rule: Move up before the bottleneck or decisive terrain, not during it. Late moves into narrow, technical, or steep features cost more energy and carry more crash risk.
On long climbs, pace near sustainable effort and avoid early surges unless the goal is selection, bridging, or covering a decisive move.
tactical_rules.level_gate: Beginners should prioritize gear choice, cadence, and non-grinding effort over racing surges.

tactical_rules.rule: Riders should plan the final portion of a climb to crest in contact or in position, because gaps can expand quickly on the descent or flat after the summit.
Descending tactics should preserve traction, sightline, braking margin, and line choice. Risk-taking is not appropriate if handling skill, weather, surface, or visibility are poor.
In crosswind, seek shelter on the leeward side, expect echelon formation, and avoid being pinned on the exposed edge of the road or group.
Headwinds increase the cost of solo riding and front exposure; use shelter where legal, keep pacing controlled, and avoid low-payoff attacks into exposed wind.
Tailwind can make high-speed attacks and breakaways harder to bring back because the chasing group receives less relative shelter benefit.
tactical_rules.backend_use: Increase attack_viability when tailwind aligns with exposed fast roads and strong riders.

tactical_rules.rule: In large fields, position before the race compresses, avoid unnecessary lateral movement, and treat front-third access as a limited resource.
In small fields, fewer riders means less hiding and fewer missed moves; racers must monitor threats and recover efficiently because every effort is more visible.
Aim to race near the front third without sitting permanently on the nose. This reduces accordion surges while avoiding unnecessary wind exposure.
A criterium corner is not finished at the apex; riders must exit smoothly, accelerate efficiently, and avoid repeated panic braking.
tactical_rules.training_connection: Include corner-entry, line choice, and repeated exit accelerations in crit-specific preparation.

tactical_rules.rule: Attacks often work better after corners, after a lull, after a prime sprint, or when the field is stretched than from predictable steady-speed sections.
A rider who is too far back before the final corners rarely fixes position in the sprint. Final-lap tactics start several laps earlier.
Begin a time trial with controlled power and fast settling into aero position rather than an unsustainable start surge.
Aero position is part of performance output. If the rider cannot hold it safely and productively, pacing targets must be adjusted.
Keep power smoother than road racing, allowing only purposeful variation for climbs, turns, descents, wind, and technical sections.
Team-pursuit rotations should balance aerodynamic shelter, rider strength, pacing, and fatigue; rotation order is tactical, not just mechanical.
Track sprint tactics require timing and position patience before maximal effort; opening too early can give the opponent a draft and timing advantage.
In track bunch events, position should preserve line, awareness, and exit options while tracking points, laps, elimination pressure, or Madison exchanges.
If passing space will disappear, move before singletrack or technical sections; forcing passes inside them wastes energy and raises crash risk.
On technical terrain, preserving momentum through line choice, braking control, and traction can beat higher peak power with poor execution.
Use cadence, body position, and torque control to preserve rear-wheel traction; standing surges can be costly if they break grip.
On smoother exposed gravel, group shelter can be decisive; on rough, loose, or narrow sectors, line choice and equipment control can matter more than draft.
Gravel tactics must include fueling, hydration, hand comfort, and mechanical risk because long rough races punish riders who treat them like short road races.
Pre-riding should identify ride-versus-run choices, tire pressure, passing zones, braking points, pit timing, and lines through mud, sand, off-camber, and barriers.
Dismount and remount quality should stay smooth under race pace; a powerful acceleration after a poor remount is usually less efficient than clean transition flow.
Pit use should consider mud accumulation, mechanical risk, tire pressure, lap timing, and position, not only whether the bike is still moving.
BMX race priority starts with gate timing, first pedal strokes, and first-straight speed because early position controls line choice into later features.
Passing attempts should account for berm entry position, exit speed, rider overlap, and next feature; forcing a pass without exit speed can lose more than it gains.
Between motos, prioritize neuromuscular freshness, track focus, and body reset rather than extra fatigue-producing riding.
In non-draft triathlon, plan pacing and overtaking around legal spacing, event-specific draft zones, and penalties rather than road-race wheel following.
Bike pacing should leave the rider able to run. Avoid heroic bike surges that create disproportionate run fade unless race context demands it.
Triathlon riders should rehearse eating and drinking in race position and at race intensity, because missed bike fueling usually damages the run.
Avoid new saddles, cleat positions, tires, aero positions, nutrition, or handling setups in the final race week unless required for safety.
tactical_rules.risk_flag: Novel equipment near an event can create fit pain, handling uncertainty, mechanical errors, or fueling problems.

tactical_rules.rule: Course recon, weather review, rule review, equipment check, and tactical rehearsal should take priority over adding fitness in the final days.
After racing, record where the rider lost contact, wasted energy, hesitated, crashed, fueled poorly, or executed well; use these facts to build the next block.
tactical_rules.backend_use: Create user-specific tactical weakness and strength records from post-event notes.

physical_demands.quality: Aerobic durability with repeated threshold, VO2, anaerobic, and sprint efforts after long time in a bunch.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Late-race decisions require enough freshness to position, cover moves, climb, descend, or sprint after prior load.

physical_demands.quality: Repeated corner-exit accelerations, short anaerobic efforts, high neuromuscular demand, and sustained concentration.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Efficient cornering reduces the need for repeated high-cost accelerations.

physical_demands.quality: Sustained high power in aerodynamic position with controlled pacing, low power variability, neck and trunk tolerance, and discipline under discomfort.
physical_demands.tactical_link: A rider who cannot hold aero position should not receive optimistic TT power targets.

physical_demands.quality: Maximal acceleration, peak power, high cadence, timing, and long recovery between high-quality sprint efforts.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Sprint tactics fail if maximal efforts are trained while fatigued or without event-specific timing.

physical_demands.quality: Aerobic-anaerobic power, aerodynamic posture, team rotation tolerance, speed control, and pacing precision.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Pursuit performance depends on matching effort distribution to rotation structure.

physical_demands.quality: High-speed bunch handling, repeated surges, tactical awareness, and sprint capacity under event-rule pressure.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Points, elimination, Madison, and scratch racing create different timing needs despite sharing the velodrome.

physical_demands.quality: Repeated high-intensity efforts, steep technical climbing, descending skill, upper-body support, braking control, and decision making under fatigue.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Skill errors can neutralize fitness; technical practice is a performance demand, not a bonus.

physical_demands.quality: High-force handling, grip, trunk and shoulder endurance, visual scanning, braking stamina, and impact tolerance.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Race pace must account for technical fatigue and crash risk, not only cardiorespiratory output.

physical_demands.quality: Long-duration endurance, vibration tolerance, fueling consistency, surface-specific cadence control, and mechanical self-management.
physical_demands.tactical_link: A strong rider can lose the event through underfueling, hand fatigue, flats, or poor line choice.

physical_demands.quality: High threshold, repeated accelerations, short running bouts, dismount/remount skill, carrying tolerance, and cornering under fatigue.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Training should pair power with transitions and surface handling instead of separating fitness from race craft.

physical_demands.quality: Gate reaction, first-straight acceleration, explosive lower-body power, pump rhythm, jump control, and repeated moto recovery.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Race position is often created before the first berm.

physical_demands.quality: Steady power, aero-position tolerance, legal spacing awareness, fueling and hydration skill, heat control, and the ability to run after the bike.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Bike effort must be judged by total race result, not only bike split rank.

physical_demands.quality: Continuous scanning, anticipation, relaxed upper body, straight-line control, braking modulation, and communication.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Riders with poor group attention should not be advanced into dense racing scenarios.

physical_demands.quality: Ability to produce sprint power after high cumulative load, positioning stress, and repeated accelerations.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Sprint workouts should eventually be trained in fatigue states that resemble event demands, while preserving technique and safety.

physical_demands.quality: Pacing, handling, fueling, clothing, and decision-making adjustment for wind, rain, heat, cold, mud, dust, and surface changes.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Weather can change the best tactic even when the course is unchanged.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Dense bunches, wheel overlap, sudden braking, poor lines, and inattention increase crash risk in road, criterium, track bunch, and gravel group situations.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Gate fast group rides and races behind handling, straight-line, scanning, and braking readiness.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Repeated high-speed corners and accelerations create fatigue-based handling errors, especially for riders sitting too far back.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Use skill-first crit sessions before adding high-density race simulations.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Long time-trial or triathlon aero position can aggravate neck, low-back, shoulder, saddle, hand, or hip discomfort.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Progress aero time gradually, monitor symptoms, and avoid race-week position changes unless safety requires it.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Wet roads, mud, loose gravel, roots, painted lines, or poor visibility increase descending and cornering crash risk.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Reduce aggressive descending tactics and prioritize braking margin, tire choice, and conservative lines.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: MTB, gravel, and cyclocross rough surfaces increase hand, wrist, forearm, shoulder, neck, and trunk load.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Track rough-surface duration and technical descent load, not only mileage or power.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Repeated big-gear, low-cadence climbing or torque-heavy gravel/MTB efforts can increase knee and tendon load in susceptible riders.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: If knee symptoms appear, reduce torque-heavy efforts, review gearing/cadence, and shift to lower intensity until stable.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Long gravel, road, MTB marathon, cyclocross race days, and triathlon bike legs can fail tactically when fueling or hydration is missed.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Treat fueling practice as a tactical readiness item for events over beginner-short durations.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Repeated unnecessary responses to attacks can overload anaerobic capacity and leave the rider unable to execute decisive later tactics.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Use race-review notes to identify impulsive chasing and prescribe tactical restraint drills.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Cyclocross run-ups, barriers, carrying, and remounts add calf, Achilles, hip, and low-back load beyond seated cycling.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Progress run-carry-remount volume gradually and avoid sudden spikes when entering CX season.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: BMX racing combines explosive starts, jumps, berms, rider contact, and repeated motos, creating high crash and neuromuscular fatigue risk.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Keep sprint quality high, protect recovery between heats, and gate technical progressions by landing and track-skill control.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Stage races, omnium-style track events, multi-day gravel, or repeated race weekends create cumulative fatigue that changes tactical reliability.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Event-week and race-weekend logic should track cumulative fatigue, sleep, travel, fueling, soreness, and residual pain.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Drafting can be illegal in many triathlon contexts and unsafe for riders without group-riding competence.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Check event draft status and rider skill readiness before recommending wheel-following, paceline, or group positioning tactics.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Untested tires, pressure, cleats, saddle, nutrition, aero bars, gearing, or bike fit near race day can cause mechanical, handling, or comfort failures.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Lock major equipment and nutrition choices before race week unless safety or rules require a change.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Heat, headwind, crosswind, and exposed courses can make target power or speed unsustainable and increase dehydration or concentration lapses.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Adjust pacing, hydration, and tactical ambition to conditions, especially in triathlon, gravel, and long road events.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: A rider with strong fitness but weak descending skill may choose tactics that exceed handling ability, particularly on unknown roads or technical MTB/gravel descents.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_response: Use skill assessment and route recon before recommending aggressive descending or high-speed technical passing.

training_implications.summary: The backend should ask discipline and event format before prescribing tactics or intensity. A road-race attack simulation, TT interval, CX transition session, BMX gate session, and triathlon bike workout are not interchangeable.
Fast group rides, pacelines, crits, and bunch races should require handling readiness: straight line, shoulder check, predictable braking, signaling, cornering, and emotional control in traffic.
Paceline progression should move from paired drafting, to small steady rotations, to larger groups, to wind-aware echelons only after control and communication are reliable.
Build race simulations around route features: final climbs, last corners, gravel sectors, singletrack entries, barriers, wind-exposed roads, feed zones, or transition exits.
Crit preparation should combine repeated accelerations, front-third positioning practice, corner-entry and exit skill, sprint timing, and decision rules for primes, attacks, and final laps.

Road-race training should include endurance durability, threshold and VO2 work, sprint-after-fatigue practice, climbing/descending tactics, breakaway simulations, and team-role rehearsal where relevant.
TT and non-draft triathlon bike work should include race-position intervals, pacing discipline, start control, wind and climb pacing, legal passing awareness, and fueling while aero.
Track plans should split sprint, pursuit, and bunch-endurance training because sprint timing, team-pursuit rotations, and points/elimination tactics are different decision systems.
MTB training should pair power with technical sections: climbing on loose surfaces, braking before turns, line choice, descending while fatigued, passing windows, and repeated hard efforts.
Gravel preparation should include long-duration fueling, equipment checks, tire and pressure decisions, rough-surface handling, exposed-road tactics, and self-sufficiency for mechanical problems.
Cyclocross training should include repeated race-pace dismounts, remounts, barriers, run-ups, corner exits, sand or mud lines, and pit decisions, layered onto threshold and anaerobic fitness.
BMX sessions should emphasize high-quality gate starts, first-straight power, pump rhythm, jumps, berm exits, and full recovery rather than endurance-style fatigue accumulation.
Triathlon bike training must account for swim and run load, brick sessions, race-legal spacing, fueling, aero tolerance, and run-preservation pacing.
Riders preparing for exposed road or gravel events should rehearse crosswind shelter, rotating echelons where safe and legal, headwind patience, and tailwind attack timing.
